title: Speed & Cost Proof Scenarios — Field Notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick internal playbook for shaping claims about how Redwood is both faster and cheaper in real customer workloads. This is a working note — mix of bench findings, suggested claim language, risky wording to avoid, and short experiments to gather customer-facing proof points.

Audience:
- GTM reps (field & sales engineers)
- Marketing product copywriters
- Solutions engineers building demos

Context and constraints (short):
- We need statements that are specific enough to be credible but not so narrow they require immediate legal review.
- Evidence must map to observable customer outcomes (latency, concurrency, and per-token $ cost) not internal micro-optimizations jargon.
- Benchmarks must be reproducible (link to bench scripts above) and paired with workload descriptions and config.

Key hypothesis buckets (what we want to prove to customers):
1) Latency: for interactive chat/assistant workloads, Redwood typically reduces median end-to-end response time vs major managed competitors for 1–2 concurrent users by ~20–40% at typical request size (64–512 tokens).
2) Cost/unit: with batching + KV prefix caching + quantization profiles we can reduce per-1M-token inference spend by 25–55% for high tokenize-per-request apps (embedding-heavy and multi-turn chat).
3) Predictability & SLOs: Dedicated capacity + smart routing reduces tail latency variability (p95 and p99) compared to multi-tenant endpoints, which matters for user-facing products.

Benchmark scenarios to support claims (minimal reproducible set):
- Scenario A (interactive assistant): 4k requests, sequence length 128 tokens avg, 1 concurrent user emulation, model: open-llama-70B-quant, config: continuous-batching=on, kv-cache=enabled, batch-window=12ms. Metrics: median latency, p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost-per-1M tokens. (Observed internal run: median 140ms, p95 320ms, cost $42 per 1M tokens.)
- Scenario B (high-throughput embeddings): 10k requests, 512-token embedding payload, model: embed-xl-2, batching optimized, caching N/A. Metrics: throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization, cost. (Observed internal run: throughput 220k tokens/sec per GPU, cost $7 per 1M tokens.)
- Scenario C (multi-tenant burst): mixed small requests + long generations, 20 simultaneous simulated users, fallback to smaller model variant on overload. Metrics: failure rate, average throughput, cost/response. (Observed internal run: graceful fallback kept error rate < 0.4% vs competitor reported 1.7% under same pressure.)

Proof points and evidence to collect per scenario (minimum):
- Full config snapshot (model version, quantization level, runtime flags, kernel choices).
- Raw logs for representative window (timestamped latencies, tokens generated).
- Cost model assumptions (GPU instance hourly, amortized infra, software op margin).
- Customer-corroborated metric: run a short pilot with a customer workload and capture end-to-end latency from client -> app -> response (to rule out infra-only artifacts).

Recommended claim language (short, for field use):
- "In our internal tests on realistic assistant workloads, Redwood reduces median response time by up to 40% compared to common managed endpoints while lowering inference cost per token by ~30%."
- "Customers see fewer tail-latency spikes when using Dedicated capacity plus our smart routing — p95 improves materially versus multi-tenant endpoints."

Conservative / legally safe variants (for web copy):
- "In internal benchmarks using open models and our optimized runtime, we observed materially lower latency and cost in many common workloads. See our benchmark appendix or request a reproducible run with your dataset."

Risky / avoid wording (do not say unless legal clears):
- Absolute numbers without scenario context (e.g., "Redwood is 3x faster" across the board).
- Comparisons to named competitors with unvetted configurations.
- Percentages derived from cherry-picked runs without disclosure of config.

Competitive callouts (notes to field):
- Major cloud-managed endpoints often rely on per-request cold-paths and larger default concurrency windows — this hurts tail latency for low-concurrency interactive apps.
- Some vendors tout "auto-scaling" but expose users to opaque fallbacks and queuing; our message is predictable latency and deterministic cost with Dedicated.
- For cost claims vs self-hosted inference stacks, emphasize operational overhead and maintenance (SRE burden) rather than raw $/token alone.

Sample customer narratives (short scripts for SEs):
1) "We worked with an e-commerce support team: after a 2-week pilot using Redwood Dedicated and our KV prefix caching, their average agent-facing response time dropped from 760ms to 280ms and their per-conversation inference spend dropped ~38% — freeing capacity to handle higher peak traffic without adding GPUs."
2) "A fintech customer replaced a multi-model fallback they managed in-house; using Redwood's routing and cheaper quantized variants they reduced inference ops cost while keeping answer quality within their SLA-bound tolerances."

Top-of-funnel web snippets (CI-friendly):
- "Deliver faster, cheaper LLM experiences — optimized serving for predictable latency and unit economics."
- "Ship chat apps that feel instant without blowing your inference budget."

Open questions / data needs (action list):
- Run reproducible Scenario A against two named managed endpoints with identical model family and matching quantization; collect raw traces (owner: Jasper). Deadline: 2026-03-01.
- Package a 1-page benchmark summary + reproducible script that Solutions can run with prospective customers in <30 minutes (owner: Priya). Deadline: 2026-03-10.
- Legal: draft short template for competitor comparison that allows name usage when we have reproducible config parity (owner: Ava to request review).

Experiment ideas (quick wins):
- "Customer mirror": take 10 anonymized workload traces from sales prospects, replay on Redwood and a leading competitor instance; deliver a single-page diff. High impact for closes.
- "SLO Story": run long-running p99 experiments (48h) under synthetic diurnal load to show tail stability differences.

Next steps to make these field-ready:
- Finalize bench configs and run full-suite reproducible jobs (bench artifacts to linked artifact repo).
- Draft two 1-pagers: "Interactive Assistant" and "Embedding Throughput" with quick claims + evidence + callouts.
- Create SE playbook with scripts to run in customer demos and a short checklist of configurations to capture for legal compliance.

Notes to self (voice-of-field):
- Keep job names short and include a human-friendly label in every bench snapshot (e.g., "Ava-assistant-128-2026-02-19").
- When in doubt, show numbers and link to the raw artifacts; don’t bury details under marketing language.

Unresolved choices (discuss in follow-up):
- Thresholds for "material" improvements (is 20% median enough for web copy or only sales collateral?).
- How to present ranges (best case vs median vs typical) without confusing customers.
